## Previously ...

You can measure what a conversion is worth (Lecture 16) and where people drop
off (Lecture 17).

. . .

One question remains, and it is the one that decides budgets:

. . .

> **Which touchpoint gets the credit?**

## The Setup

A visitor:

1. Sees an Instagram post
2. Two days later, searches your brand name and clicks the organic result
3. A week later, clicks a paid search ad
4. Converts

. . .

Four touchpoints. One conversion. **How do you split the credit?**

. . .

There is no correct answer. There are only models, and models are assumptions.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Describe the main attribution models and what each assumes
- Explain why models disagree, and by how much
- Judge which model suits a given business
- Distinguish attribution from incrementality

# 1. Rule-Based Models

## Last Click

All credit to the final touchpoint before conversion.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why it survived**

- Simple to compute
- Requires no cross-session tracking
- Auditable, reproducible, hard to game accidentally
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**What it assumes**

That nothing before the last click mattered.

Which systematically over-credits brand search, retargeting and email, and
under-credits everything at the top.
:::
::::

. . .

Still the default in most reporting, and still the model most budget decisions
are quietly made on.

## First Click

All credit to the first touchpoint.

. . .

The mirror image: over-credits discovery, ignores everything that closed the sale.

. . .

Useful mainly as a **contrast case**. Running both first and last click and
comparing is more informative than either alone.

## Linear, Time Decay, Position Based

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Linear**

Equal credit to all touchpoints.

Assumes every contact mattered the same. At least it is neutral.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Time decay**

More credit the closer to conversion.

Assumes recency equals influence. Reasonable for short cycles, wrong for long ones.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Position based**

40% first, 40% last, 20% split between.

Assumes discovery and closing matter most. The 40/40/20 is arbitrary.
:::
::::

. . .

Notice that each of these encodes a **theory of how marketing works**, chosen
before any data was seen.

## The Honest Description

A rule-based attribution model is a **budgeting convention**, not a measurement.

. . .

It divides credit according to a rule you picked. Changing the rule changes the
answer without any change in the world.

# 2. Data-Driven Attribution

## What It Does

GA4's default model. Rather than applying a fixed rule, it compares:

- Conversion paths that **included** a touchpoint
- Conversion paths that **did not**

. . .

and assigns credit in proportion to the estimated marginal contribution, using a
Shapley-value style approach borrowed from cooperative game theory.

## Why It Is Better

- Credit is derived from your data, not from a rule
- It can detect that a channel appears in many paths but changes few outcomes
- It adapts as behaviour changes

. . .

It is, genuinely, a better answer to the question "which channels appear in
paths that convert".

## Why It Is Not the Answer

<!-- Speaker notes: students will take DDA as the "correct" model because it is
     the default and it sounds scientific. Push hard here. -->

. . .

**It is still correlational.** It compares paths that happened. It does not
compare a world where you advertised to one where you did not.

. . .

**It is a black box.** You cannot audit it, reproduce it, or explain it to a
client in detail.

. . .

**It needs volume.** GA4 requires substantial conversion data before DDA is
available. Your portfolio will not qualify.

. . .

**It cannot see what it cannot track.** Which is the next section.

## What No Model Can See

- Touchpoints where consent was declined (Lecture 4)
- Cross-device journeys with no login
- Offline exposure: outdoor, print, radio, word of mouth
- Views without clicks: the Instagram post they saw and never tapped
- Anyone using a browser that blocks the tag

. . .

**Attribution models divide credit among the touchpoints you happened to
record.** Everything else gets zero by construction.

# 3. Why the Models Disagree

## A Worked Comparison

Same 100 conversions, five models:

| Channel | Last click | First click | Linear | Time decay | Data-driven |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Paid search | 42 | 18 | 27 | 35 | 24 |
| Organic search | 24 | 21 | 23 | 24 | 22 |
| Social | 9 | 34 | 21 | 14 | 27 |
| Email | 19 | 6 | 15 | 18 | 13 |
| Direct | 6 | 21 | 14 | 9 | 14 |

. . .

**Social gets 9 conversions or 34, depending on which column you read.** Nothing
about the world changed.

## The Practical Consequence

Whoever chooses the model chooses the budget.

. . .

This is why attribution arguments in agencies are rarely technical arguments.

. . .

The defensible position is not "my model is right". It is: **here is the range
across models, here is why they differ, and here is the decision that is robust
across all of them.**

# 4. Beyond Attribution

## The Incrementality Question

Attribution asks: **of the conversions that happened, who gets credit?**

. . .

The business question is different: **how many of these conversions would have
happened anyway?**

. . .

Brand search converts at 30% and shows a 12x ROAS. Most of those people were
already going to buy. Attribution cannot tell you that. It was never designed to.

## How Incrementality Is Actually Measured

- **Geo holdouts**: turn a channel off in one region, compare
- **Audience holdouts**: withhold a campaign from a randomised group
- **Ghost ads / PSA tests**: serve a placebo to the control group
- **Marketing mix modelling**: regress outcomes on spend at aggregate level

. . .

Every one of these is an **experiment or a model**, not an attribution report.
Lectures 19 and 19.

## Where This Leaves You

For your portfolio:

- You will not have enough conversions for data-driven attribution
- You will probably not have multi-touch paths at all
- **Say so.** Report last click, state the limitation, and explain what you would
  do with more volume

. . .

That is a stronger answer than a confident multi-touch analysis on eight
conversions.

# 5. Asking AI to Argue Each Model

## An Ideal Use Case

<!-- Speaker notes: attribution is contested, well documented, and has no
     correct answer. That is exactly the shape of question where an assistant
     generating the competing cases is more useful than one giving an answer. -->

Attribution arguments are arguments. An assistant is good at producing the case
for a position it does not hold.

. . .

> "Argue that we should credit social with these conversions. Then argue that we
> should not. Then tell me what evidence would settle it."

## Where It Helps

- Producing the case each stakeholder would make for their own channel
- Explaining Shapley-value attribution in language a client will follow
- Writing the code for the model comparison table
- Listing what your data cannot see

## Where It Will Mislead You

**It will pick a model if you ask it to.** It has no basis for doing so. The
choice depends on your business, your sales cycle and your channel mix, none of
which it knows.

. . .

**It will not volunteer that your sample is too small** for multi-touch analysis
unless you ask.

. . .

**It will describe data-driven attribution as more rigorous** without noting that
it is still correlational. Lecture 18's whole argument.

## The Prompt Worth Keeping

> "Here is my conversion path data [attached]. Build the comparison table across
> last click, first click, linear and time decay. Then tell me which budget
> decisions are the same under all four models, and which flip."

. . .

That last clause is the analysis. The table is just arithmetic.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

2. Ask it which decisions are robust across models and which are not
3. Check one channel's last-click credit by hand
4. Ask it to argue for the model you did not choose, and note the best point it makes
